n: Moved by her description, the women ask where her beloved has gone so they can help her look.
She knows where he is: in his garden among the spices and lilies. The garden again stands for their shared love.
She restates their bond: she belongs to him and he to her. The love is fully mutual.

f.w: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine
f.r: Song of Solomon 2:16; Song of Solomon 7:10

n: He praises her as beautiful as Tirzah and lovely as Jerusalem — two royal cities — and as awe-inspiring as an army with banners flying.

f.g: A beautiful city whose name means “pleasing”; later capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23).

n: Her eyes overwhelm him so much he asks her to look away. He repeats earlier praises of her hair.

f.w: thy hair is as a flock of goats

n: He repeats his praise of her bright, even teeth.
Her cheeks behind her veil are like slices of pomegranate.
A king might have sixty queens, eighty concubines, and countless maidens.

f.g: Secondary wives in ancient royal households.

n: But his dove, his perfect one, is unique — her mother’s favorite. Even queens and the other women praise her. To him, she is the only one.
Others exclaim: who is this who shines like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, and majestic as an army? D&C 5:14, 105:31, and 109:73 apply this language to the latter-day Church.

f.w: fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners

n: Someone — probably the bride — went down to the walnut grove to see if the valley’s vines and pomegranates had begun to bloom.
Before she knew it, her desire carried her away as if in a royal chariot. The Hebrew is very difficult, and translations vary widely.

f.g: Possibly “my noble people”; the meaning is uncertain.

n: Others call her back: “Come back, Shulamite, so we can see you.” She asks why they would gaze at her as at a festive dance.

f.g: Possibly “woman of Shulem/Shunem,” or a feminine form of Solomon’s name — “the Solomon-ess.”
Or “the dance of Mahanaim” — a joyful dance.
